shared_text:
The flight. A twin-engine airliner on an airline flight, departing a large airport neither pilot used regularly. Visual conditions, gusty winds.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring. The captain had about 160 hours on type.

What happened. Cleared for the published departure to 2,500 ft, the crew briefed a hand-flown departure in heading mode. At 400 ft the captain began the published left turn to heading 190. The instruction the crew received from the departure controller was to turn left to heading 300 and climb to 10,000 ft. The first officer read it back and set it; the captain checked. The captain said that, though not certain, it seemed non-standard, perhaps to take them over the airport, so they would keep flaps 1 and 210 knots for a tight turn and steep climb. About 30 seconds later the controller asked why they were turning left and ordered an immediate right turn to heading 270. Startled, and anxious that they had deviated, the captain rolled right. The first officer called out the bank, which reached about 45 degrees, and the "bank angle" alert sounded twice. A second controller ordered them to stop the climb immediately; the captain levelled off and had 3,000 ft set. As the speed rose towards 250 knots, the captain saw the flaps were still at 1 and called for flaps up. Neither pilot saw the speed pass 250 knots, and there was no overspeed warning.
safe_outcome: Air traffic control then vectored the aircraft back to heading 300 and out of the departure airspace, and the flight continued. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Removed under rule 3: the captain's later belief that the controllers had given the wrong initial instruction and so never followed it up; the captain's view that startle and stress 'contributed to my over reaction' and the question 'Why did I over control the aircraft?'; the four hours of self-debriefing, 'our mistakes' and 'very embarrassing'; the aside that the flap point 'will be very relevant later'; the captain's reading of 'please keep turning' as implying non-compliance. Kept as facts at the time: the crew's unfamiliarity with the airport, the hand-flown heading-mode briefing, the instruction as the crew received it and its readback, the captain's doubt about it and reason for keeping flaps 1 and 210 knots, the startle and the captain's anxiety (a state reported at the time), the bank of about 45 degrees and the two bank angle alerts, the stop-climb order and level-off, and the late flap retraction with no observed flap overspeed. Moved to the safe ending (rule 5): the vectors back to heading 300 and out of the airspace. The flight attendants' later report of no injuries is covered by the fixed ending line. Removed under rule 6: the airport, departure name, runway, intersection and frequency. Judgement calls: the report does not show whether the controller actually said 'left heading 300', so the text says only that this was the instruction the crew received; the type is not given ('commercial fixed wing'), so 'twin-engine airliner' was used; the light is not given (local time band 1201-1800, January), so day or night is not stated; cut for length: the chart and threat review (including company notes on avoiding lateral navigation mode), 'expect vectors', the maximum-thrust take-off, the first officer setting the new heading, the level-change mode, the after take-off checklist call, and a controller's request to 'please keep turning' (its timing in the sequence is unclear); the shared text runs to the flap retraction, which came after the stop-climb order, because it is a crew action in the same sequence and leaving it out of one version only would make the versions differ. The report shows no traffic, so the standard safe-ending line is used. Bracket 'crossing' because the deviation was a turn the opposite way from the one controllers expected, across other airspace, followed by an order to stop climbing.
